title: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence
pub: Yale Law & Policy Review, vol. 43, no. 1, pp. 95-170 (2024)
author: Tejas N. Narechania · Ganesh Sitaraman

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source does not assess whether human oversight provides effective control, independent verification or expertise development. It instead reframes AI governance around market structure, arguing that antimonopoly tools should be incorporated early because concentration may contribute to harms such as bias and privacy problems.
qs: may in fact inhibit innovation; and that some of the most prominent worries about AI—such as bias and privacy—might themselves be partly the result of market structure concerns.
As policymakers debate governing AI at this early stage in its technological lifecycle, antimonopoly tools must be part of the conversation.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source does not assess legal-workflow productivity, verification, competence or lawyer replacement. Instead, it shifts the governance focus to an underexamined issue: competition and concentration in AI supply chains and infrastructure.
qs: To the extent there has been such discussion, it has largely focused on       semiconductor manufacturing, and to a lesser extent, cloud-infrastructure       provision.
But even then, these concerns have not generally been considered       in the context of AI specifically.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess task-level legal-AI capability, human verification or workflow redesign. It instead reframes AI governance around concentration and vertical integration across the industrial stack, treating market structure and antimonopoly intervention as the central priorities.
qs: Our focus here is on market concentration and its harms.
But we believe that our        account is the first comprehensive assessment of the market structure of the        entire stack, from microprocessing hardware to applications.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The excerpt reports the EU AI Act, industry calls for regulation or a development pause, and scholarly concern about AI harms. It does not state the author’s own position or assess how simplification, risk differentiation, standards, or implementation can produce enforceable safeguards without unduly restricting adoption.

st.t: Regulatory institutions: Governance needs implementation markets
st.an: The source accepts the need for proactive governance institutions and materially extends the cluster by treating AI market structure as both a regulatory target and a precondition for effective implementation. It proposes ex ante antimonopoly tools, including interoperability and constraints on infrastructure bottlenecks, while cautioning that open models alone cannot overcome hardware and cloud concentration.
qs: The Advantages of Ex Ante Governance      Our analysis of the AI technology stack and its market structure— coupled with an assessment of current law—also suggests that ex ante governance solutions are essential tools and important complements to ex post antitrust enforcement on a case-by-case basis.
Moreover, our analysis of the AI technology stack shows that open-source models will not address the unregulated AI oligopoly at the hardware or cloud layers.

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition: capital, data, compute and vertical integration create strong concentration pressures, but it frames outcomes conditionally rather than establishing inevitable monopoly. It also acknowledges productive-efficiency benefits while showing why open models do not by themselves remove dependence on concentrated cloud and hardware infrastructure.
qs: which in some cases lack the capital required.”110 As a result, the number of foundation models that can (or that perhaps should, from the standpoint of productive efficiency) exist for any given application class—language, image generation—may be quite limited.111

Third, and relatedly, without a significant change in the industrial organization of those layers, any open-source AI foundation model will be dependent on an oligopoly of the biggest technology companies.

kp.k: AI governance requires attention to industrial organization
kp.d: The authors offer a legal-policy framework for governing concentration throughout the AI supply chain, rather than an empirical study of legal employment or law-firm organization. They distinguish four layers—hardware, cloud infrastructure, models, and applications—with data and model access nested within the model layer. Their central argument is that apparent diversity among applications can conceal dependence on a small group of upstream providers. They explicitly limit their project to concentration and its harms rather than comprehensive AI governance.
qs: But a closer look reveals that a small oligopoly of large and well-entrenched players controls the technologies on which these applications are based.
Our focus here is on market concentration and its harms.

kp.k: Hardware concentration creates critical upstream bottlenecks
kp.d: Drawing on industry reports rather than original market measurement, the article reports Nvidia's estimated share of AI GPU chips as between 80 and 95 percent. It identifies TSMC as the dominant fabricator, Samsung as the other producer of similarly advanced chips, and ASML as the sole supplier of equipment needed for the smallest chips. High capital requirements and technological sophistication underpin the authors' expectation that concentration will persist. These are historical estimates assembled for the 2024 article, not present-day market shares.
qs: While reports differ, Nvidia—which designs chips—appears to have captured between 80 and 95 percent market share of the GPU chip business used for AI.
Apart from TSMC, only Samsung fabricates similarly small, high-powered chips.

kp.k: Cloud infrastructure combines scale economies with customer lock-in
kp.d: The authors identify high capital costs, network effects, provider-specific expertise, technical switching burdens, and egress fees as mechanisms sustaining cloud oligopoly. Their cited estimates place AWS above 30 percent, approaching 40 percent in some assessments, and Azure near 20 percent, with Google Cloud further behind. They report that some businesses consider even a twenty percent price discount insufficient to justify switching. Market boundaries and estimates vary by analyst and year.
qs: Some businesses have declared that even a twenty percent price discount is insufficient to overcome these concerns.
The more users on a single cloud system, the more developers will make applications designed for that cloud system, which, in turn, attracts more users.

kp.k: Data and compute costs constrain foundation-model entry
kp.d: Foundation-model development requires financing for data acquisition, preparation, and computationally intensive training. The authors distinguish freely accessible raw data from usable, licensed, proprietary, or debiased data, which can be costly. They argue that these barriers could limit the number of foundation models per application class. For some continually learning systems, deployment generates additional relevant data, potentially reinforcing first-mover advantages; they do not assert that this mechanism applies equally to every model.
qs: Developing a foundation model often requires substantial capital investment.

Moreover, there may be significant data-network effects for some models, particularly for models and applications that rely on forms of deep, continual, or reinforcement learning, giving rise to significant first-mover advantages.

kp.k: Application entry differs from economically sustainable scaling
kp.d: The article distinguishes vertically integrated applications, unaffiliated applications using proprietary models through APIs, and applications using open-source models. Patent drafting and analysis applications illustrate the proprietary-API category. Although application development and individual inference calls can be relatively inexpensive compared with model training, large-scale inference still requires substantial resources. Open-source application developers may remain dependent on dominant hardware and cloud suppliers.
qs: For example, some developers are using OpenAI’s documented APIs to develop specific applications based upon GPT, such as patent drafting and analysis applications.
This means that though developing an application might be comparatively cheap, scaling its use may prove to be very expensive.

kp.k: Vertical integration enables discrimination but may offer efficiencies
kp.d: The authors predict that integrated providers could favor affiliated applications through prices, early model access, distribution, or exclusion of rivals. They distinguish monopoly, structurally separated competition, and vertically integrated competition as alternative market structures. However, they acknowledge possible engineering and performance benefits from integrating chips, cloud infrastructure, and inference applications, leaving the appropriate boundary partly unresolved and recommending technically informed regulatory judgment.
qs: At the extreme, model providers might exclude some third-party applications from using the model altogether, thereby preventing any competition with the affiliated application.
It is true that these concerns must be weighed against the possible benefits of vertical integration.
The answer to this question remains uncertain, and it is somewhat hard to disentangle the providers’ technical arguments favoring integration from their economic incentives

kp.k: Concentration threatens prices and propagates model-quality problems
kp.d: The article identifies potential monopoly pricing, discriminatory supply, and reduced quality competition across the stack. It distinguishes hypothetical misconduct by ASML from reported TSMC prioritization of Apple and cited cloud-provider pricing concerns. At the model layer, the authors argue that limited alternatives could weaken incentives to improve quality while transmitting shared model defects across many applications. These mechanisms are not presented as measured AI-sector causal effects.
qs: While it is not obvious that ASML has taken any of these actions so far, these strategies are often deployed by monopolists, to the detriment of the market.
If there are only one or two models in an application class (e.g., text, images) and those are flawed, then every application built on those models will suffer from those flaws.

kp.k: Copying and acquisitions can deter downstream innovation
kp.d: Drawing on complaints concerning AWS, scholarship on strategic acquisitions, and economic models of platform kill zones, the authors argue that upstream providers can appropriate downstream innovations or acquire potential challengers. The prospect of copying, foreclosure, or limited investment upside can discourage entrepreneurs and venture investors before entry occurs. The extension of these mechanisms to foundation-model-dependent applications is an argument by analogy and prediction, not a measured finding about legal-AI startups.
qs: Multiple firms have complained that AWS has copied their product and offered their own integrated version of the product, harming their company’s value and future business.
Similar concerns attend to applications built upon foundation models.
The model developers might appropriate the application and integrate its features into its own offerings.

kp.k: Infrastructure concentration creates systemic resilience risks
kp.d: The authors connect semiconductor geographic concentration to exposure to pandemics, severe weather, and conflict, particularly risks involving Taiwan. Cloud concentration and poor interoperability can turn outages or cyberattacks into cascading disruptions. They also use hypothetical medical and military examples to explain how reliance on a single flawed foundation model could produce correlated failures. They recommend greater supplier and geographic diversity and warn that concentrated procurement can increase costs and weaken quality.
qs: Concentration leads to a fragile supply chain that is vulnerable to single points of failure across the stack.
The lack of interoperability means that these systems could not easily be restarted on another provider’s service.
An unregulated AI oligopoly will also focus primarily on economically profitable activities—activities that might not align with public goods or national security needs.

kp.k: Concentration may deepen economic and political inequalities
kp.d: The authors predict that concentrated ownership will channel AI returns toward a small group of firms, executives, and shareholders, and toward countries hosting dominant providers. They connect extraction of data from other economies to global inequality and discuss cultural risks from predominantly English-based systems. Their democracy argument concerns concentrated corporate control of information and the political influence of wealth, supported by broader political-science literature rather than an AI-specific causal study.
qs: First, concentration means that a small number of firms will capture the vast majority of the financial returns in this sector.

Second, concentration in AI is likely to increase global inequality, as the dominant firms, located in a small number of industrialized and technologized countries, extract value from data that is harvested from other economies.
Economic power also often translates into political power.

kp.k: Stable structural risks justify regulation before technical maturity
kp.d: Rejecting the pacing-problem objection, the authors argue that rapid improvements in AI capabilities do not eliminate identifiable and relatively stable concentration mechanisms. They invoke the Collingridge Dilemma: delaying intervention until a technology is better understood can allow its proponents to acquire enough power to obstruct regulation. They nevertheless allow for uncertainty about particular remedies, such as separation between chips and cloud infrastructure.
qs: The pace of technological development does not affect these fundamentals or the harms that flow from them.
Moreover, declining to regulate in view of ongoing technological development threatens to forestall regulation altogether.

kp.k: Ex ante governance should complement antitrust enforcement
kp.d: The authors retain a role for antitrust but argue that case-specific, retrospective enforcement is insufficient for an already concentrated sector. They discuss restrictive US doctrines governing predatory pricing, price squeezes, refusals to deal, and essential facilities, alongside litigation delay, agency resource constraints, and commercial disincentives to sue infrastructure suppliers. They favor prospective rules and agency expertise as more adaptable means of shaping markets before exclusion and lock-in become entrenched.
qs: Antitrust enforcement can be a powerful antimonopoly tool to address specific problems with abuses of market power and to shape markets and create deterrence.

The ex post nature of antitrust enforcement undermines effective governance in the AI sector because it allows consolidation to accrue and abusive practices to take place—potentially for years—before they may be redressed.

kp.k: Structural regulation can support innovation and conduct safeguards
kp.d: Against the claim that regulation necessarily impedes innovation, the authors argue that neutral access to infrastructure can protect downstream entry and experimentation, citing internet regulation as an historical analogy. Mapping the stack can also identify more effective intervention points for bias, privacy, and inaccurate outputs, including data processing and models rather than applications alone. They expressly qualify the argument: competition is not guaranteed to cure conduct harms, and upstream licensing or liability requirements could themselves raise entry barriers.
qs: In short, we think the structural approach is an essential complement to conduct-based regulations.
We do not mean to suggest competition or regulation is sure to address concerns about conduct harms like algorithmic bias and discrimination.
But market structure interventions may be critically important complements to regulations that seek to directly address concerns about bias, discrimination, and privacy.

kp.k: Open-source models cannot independently eliminate upstream market power
kp.d: The authors give four reasons for skepticism: openness varies across releases; model availability does not decentralize hardware or cloud infrastructure; upstream incumbents can discriminate against or absorb open-source-based businesses; and open-source strategies can reinforce incumbent ecosystems. They cite the LLaMA 3.1 license's requirement of Meta approval for applications serving more than 700 million users and historical examples involving Android, cloud databases, and AI frameworks. Their conclusion is conditional, not a rejection of open-source development's value.
qs: First, “open source” is not a binary between open and closed, but rather a spectrum.
The existence of open-source models does not address concentration in these other, lower layers.
In short, open source can be used to disrupt dominant platforms—but it can also be used by dominant firms to extend their platforms and entrench their status.

kp.k: Industrial policy should diversify suppliers rather than entrench incumbents
kp.d: The authors support semiconductor industrial policy for resilience while urging competition-sensitive grant and procurement decisions. They report that the Chips and Science Act of 2022 committed $52.7 billion to semiconductor programs across Commerce, Defense, and the National Science Foundation. They argue that subsidies directed to dominant firms may extend incumbency, whereas support for smaller entrants may diversify supply. They describe the competition effects of these policies as unresolved and cite the November 2, 2023 draft OMB memorandum as an emerging procurement approach.
qs: One of the central questions for industrial policy in the AI sector is whether investment decisions will entrench dominant players or facilitate competition.
It is too early to tell whether U.S. industrial policies will entrench power or increase competition

kp.k: Utility-style rules could constrain infrastructure gatekeeping
kp.d: Proposed networks, platforms, and utilities tools include separating cloud providers from higher layers, nondiscrimination, open access, transparent uniform pricing, and potentially regulated rates. The authors regard structural separation as easier to administer for self-preferencing than ongoing monitoring of conduct. They explain that access and pricing rules may still be needed for separated providers because separation alone does not prevent exclusion or excessive charges. Proposed applications span chip supply, cloud services, commercial data resources, foundation models, and APIs.
qs: Perhaps most notably, structurally separating the cloud layer from higher layers in the stack could address a wide range of market dominance problems identified above.
Equal-pricing rules are an essential corollary to open access because firms could otherwise charge prohibitive prices to undermine nondiscriminatory access requirements.
Structural separations, by contrast, are prophylactic: They prevent any commingling of business lines and thus can be more easily administered.

kp.k: Interoperability could reduce switching costs and data advantages
kp.d: Using telephone interconnection and number portability as analogies, the authors propose cloud interoperability and common APIs to ease movement between infrastructure and model suppliers. They also propose federated-learning requirements that allow participating applications to share model improvements while retaining training data locally. These are prospective interventions, not demonstrated AI-market outcomes; the article acknowledges unresolved personal-data and reliable-anonymization issues.
qs: One type of interoperability rule would be to mandate data sharing through federated learning.
Instead, the model’s improvements are derived from all the applications that use it—and are shared among all of them, too.
A common API, used across providers, could lower that developer’s switching costs and thereby yield greater competition.

kp.k: Public options require genuine alternatives to incumbent provision
kp.d: The authors propose public cloud capacity and public datasets to discipline private prices, improve resilience, and support research or uses that commercial providers may underserve. They cite Japan's planned public supercomputer and examine the proposed National AI Research Resource and CREATE AI Act of 2023. They caution that publicly funded access purchased from existing oligopolists may reinforce rather than counter concentration, distinguishing a genuinely public option from subsidized private supply.
qs: Public options are publicly provided goods or services that coexist with private-market options, offered at some (often regulatorily) set price.

The NAIRR, if funded, should ensure it is a true public option, rather than a government contract for researchers to purchase compute and other resources from oligopolistic cloud providers while further entrenching them.

kp.k: Cooperative ownership could align AI provision with users
kp.d: Drawing on historical utility governance and cooperative enterprise scholarship, the authors propose user-owned alternatives to investor-controlled AI infrastructure. Possibilities include a research cloud owned by universities, nonprofits, and government, user-governed foundation models, and ownership stakes earned through data contributions. They argue that cooperatives could redirect excess returns to users, limit extraction, expand access, and reflect member values. These are governance proposals rather than evaluated AI-sector implementations.
qs: Cooperative governance shifts management’s priorities from distant shareholders toward users of the firm, with any excess profit going back to those same users.
Rather than concentrate wealth among the shareholders of a platform business, cooperatives distribute wealth across the user-owners.

One might even imagine a cooperative model where one earns stakes in a model or application by contributing data to its development—or alternatively, a cooperative-governance approach to a foundation model, in which users govern the model.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Narechania and Sitaraman argue that concentration across AI infrastructure creates durable oligopoly risks and that proactive antimonopoly governance could improve competition, innovation, resilience, and the distribution of benefits.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about AI industrial organization and governance, not a study of changes in lawyers’ employment or legal-service delivery. The authors describe concentration in hardware and cloud services, substantial entry barriers in foundation models, and vertical integration across the stack. They predict that these conditions will sustain dominant providers and enable high prices, reduced quality competition, self-preferencing, exclusion, copying of downstream products, acquisitions that absorb potential competitors, and vendor lock-in. These practices may deter downstream investment and innovation. Concentration also creates correlated infrastructure and model failures, concentrates wealth, and gives a few firms disproportionate influence over information and politics. Their proposed responses include competition-sensitive industrial policy, structural separation, nondiscrimination and open access, rate regulation, interoperability, public options, and cooperative ownership. They argue that these interventions can encourage downstream innovation and complement measures targeting bias, privacy, and accuracy. Open-source models alone, they contend, cannot resolve concentration in underlying hardware and cloud infrastructure and can sometimes reinforce incumbent platforms. The article mentions patent-drafting and analysis applications built on proprietary models as an example of downstream development, but offers no legal-sector productivity or displacement prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims through synthesis of market reports, technical research, reported business conduct, economic theory, historical regulatory examples, and legal doctrine—not an original empirical test of the proposed AI policies.
pts.d: For existing concentration, the article cites estimates, principally from 2022–2023 reporting, that Nvidia held 80–95% of the AI GPU market; a 2022 foundry-market estimate places TSMC at 58.5% and Samsung at 15.8%; ASML is identified as the sole supplier of the equipment needed for the most advanced photolithography. Cloud market reports place AWS above 30%, Azure near 20%, and Google behind them. Technical and industry sources describe large training costs, data requirements, scale economies, switching costs, egress fees, and network effects. The authors cite congressional investigations and Ofcom’s 2023 cloud study for competition concerns. Reports of AWS copying downstream products, TSMC prioritizing Apple, and Microsoft threatening restrictions on rival AI search tools illustrate mechanisms of discrimination or appropriation; not all are demonstrated AI-specific harms. Economic modelling of platform 'kill zones' supports the investment-deterrence argument. Historical telecommunications regulation and number portability support the proposed benefits of separation and interoperability by analogy. Predatory-pricing, price-squeeze, refusal-to-deal, and essential-facilities decisions support their argument that prevailing antitrust doctrine may be insufficient. Broader political-science and inequality research underpins their distributional and democratic concerns. Public options and cooperative AI governance are proposals supported primarily by institutional reasoning and experience in other sectors, rather than measured AI implementation outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article presents concentration as already observable in 2024 and likely to persist, without specifying a quantified forecast horizon; its predictions depend on infrastructure economics, integration, and regulatory choices.
pts.d: The authors distinguish existing infrastructure concentration from potential future abuses and consolidation. They argue that rapid technical progress does not eliminate sufficiently stable market-structure features to justify waiting for regulation. Their principal counterfactual is continued unregulated oligopoly: under that condition, market power, barriers to entry, inequality, and political influence may become more entrenched. Model-level concentration and data feedback advantages are qualified by application class, compute needs, and whether systems learn from deployment. They acknowledge that vertical integration may offer technical benefits, especially between chips and cloud infrastructure, and leave its net desirability unresolved. They do not propose abandoning antitrust enforcement, but supplementing it with ex ante tools. They explicitly do not claim that greater competition or structural regulation will necessarily solve bias, discrimination, or privacy problems. Their skepticism toward open-source competition concerns its sufficiency without changes to lower-layer industrial organization, not the absence of any value from openness. Industrial policy’s competitive effects depend on whether funding diversifies suppliers or entrenches incumbents; a public research resource must offer a genuine alternative rather than simply subsidize purchases from incumbent clouds. Cooperative models remain prospective institutional options. The article focuses on concentration and its harms rather than comprehensive AI governance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify downstream developers, infrastructure users, researchers, consumers, governments, and the wider public as exposed to concentrated AI supply chains, while incumbent firms and their owners may capture disproportionate benefits.
pts.d: Independent model and application developers face dependence on upstream suppliers that may also compete against them, potentially increasing input prices, restricting access, copying products, and discouraging investment. Open-source developers remain dependent on concentrated compute and hardware markets. Researchers, universities, nonprofits, and startups may lack affordable access to compute and training data; public or cooperative infrastructure is proposed to expand their options. Consumers and businesses may face higher prices, fewer alternatives, persistent model defects, and difficulty switching providers. Government, military, financial-sector, medical, and other critical-infrastructure users face correlated outages or errors and limited alternative suppliers. Dominant firms, executives, engineers, and shareholders may capture outsized financial returns, while countries outside the leading AI economies may supply data without receiving comparable benefits. The authors also identify potential risks to linguistic diversity and democratic debate. Cooperative ownership is proposed to give users more control over services and a greater share of returns. Patent-application developers are a specific example of dependent downstream vendors; the article does not separately assess law firms, in-house counsel, ALSPs, or access to justice.
